---
title: "Getting started"
subtitle: "One comparison, start to finish"
---
<<dd_version: 2>>

Every `mecompare` analysis has the same three steps: fit the models, store them,
compare. This page runs through one example with Stata's `nlsw88` data and then
explains how to read the table.

## 1. Fit and store the models

The question: does the association between having a college degree and union
membership change once we account for wages and work experience? Fit the model
without those variables, then the model with them, storing each with
`estimates store`.

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
sysuse nlsw88, clear
drop if missing(union)

quietly logit union i.collgrad c.age i.south i.smsa, vce(robust)
estimates store base

quietly logit union i.collgrad c.age i.south i.smsa c.wage c.ttl_exp, vce(robust)
estimates store full
<</dd_do>>
```

Nothing here is specific to `mecompare`; any estimation command that works with
`margins` can be used, and `vce(robust)` is recommended because the models will
be combined with `suest2`.

## 2. Compare the marginal effects

Name the variable whose effect you want and the stored models in `models()`.

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
mecompare i.collgrad, models(base full)
<</dd_do>>
```

## 3. Read the table

Each block of the table is one marginal effect. For a binary or factor variable
the effect is the discrete change in the predicted probability between its
levels; for a continuous variable it is the change for a one-unit increase
(other amounts are set with `amount()`). Within a block:

- the first rows give the marginal effect in each model, in the order the
  models were listed in `models()`;
- the **Difference** row is the effect in the first model minus the effect in
  the second, with a standard error and p-value that account for the fact
  that both effects were estimated from the same data.

The `#` column numbers the rows so that you can refer to them in
[`metest`](../metest/index.html) for any other contrast.

## Continuous variables and the size of the change

For a continuous variable, `amount()` sets the size of the change. Here the
effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in age:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
mecompare age, models(base full) amount(sd)
<</dd_do>>
```

## Comparing effects within one model

With a single model in `models()`, `mecompare` reports the marginal effects of
the variables listed, and `metest` compares them. Here, is the union-membership
gap by college degree the same size as the gap by region?

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
mecompare i.collgrad i.south, models(full)
metest 1 - 2
<</dd_do>>
```

## Frequently used options

The help file (`help mecompare`) documents everything; these are the options
that come up most often.

| Option | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `models(name1 [name2])` | The stored estimates to compare. One model gives marginal effects for that model alone. |
| `amount()` | Size of the change for a continuous variable: a number, `sd` or `2sd` (one or two standard deviations), or `rate` (the instantaneous rate of change). |
| `start()` | Where the change in a continuous variable begins: `start(varname=#)` or `start(atmeans)`. |
| `covariates(varname=# ...)`, `atmeans` | Hold other variables at specified values or at their means (the default averages over the observed values). |
| `by(varlist)` | Marginal effects within each level of another variable, in one table, so that they can be compared with `metest`. |
| `over(varlist)` | Marginal effects within subsamples defined by another variable. |
| `pwcompare` | All pairwise contrasts among the levels of a nominal variable, not just contrasts with the base level. |
| `groups` | The models were fit to separate groups (see the [groups example](examples/groups.html)). |
| `totalme`, `meinequality` | Add the Total Marginal Effect or the marginal-effect inequality summary for the compared effects. |
| `store(stub)` | Store the results so that they can be graphed with `coefplot` or tabled with `esttab`. |
